items.title: Henry A. "Hank" Kmen Interview, 1963-02-13
items.q: although they would have a genius like Gottschall, of course he left New Orleans when he was 10 or 11 years old to study for all the next years in France

ctx.x: Negro wider feel. Well that condition exists until today, I mean really, the Negro bands play for both races, the white bands don't play for white. Yes. Well that brings up the point with me now, at what period did you say it became more fashionable for a man to go into business, a white band to go into business? Well there was some feeling about this all the way through,

you see, in the early, oh in the 1820s and the 1830s and 40s, families tended to discourage a man who thought of taking up the piano or something, although they would have a genius like Gottschall, of course he left New Orleans when he was 10 or 11 years old to study for all the next years in France, the 1860s until he came back. But very few white men in New Orleans aspire to become, say, a performer in the orchestra of the French theater. But what happened to keep a lot of white musicians around and even…

This is Reel 2, Henry Command, February 13th, 1963. We were talking there about the white musicians and how you had their replacements at the French opera. And what I was really getting at was in the early jazz days, and I don't know how much we know about that, but judging from the memories of people like Jack Lang, which is maybe even pre-jazz as we know it.
